title: Three ticking clocks threaten Sri Lanka’s digital future: Deputy Minister | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:26
-     - 152

Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne delivering the keynote at Daily FT-CICRA Cyber Security Summit inauguration – Pic by Ruwan Walpola

By Hiyal Biyagamage

Sri Lanka faces three critical cybersecurity challenges, described as the “attacker’s clock”, “quantum clock” and “trust clock”, Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne warned, stressing that the country’s digital transformation depends on its ability to respond to increasingly sophisticated cyber threats while maintaining public confidence.

Addressing the 12th Cyber Security Summit organised by the Daily FT and CICRA, Eng. Weeraratne said the three clocks were moving at different speeds, exposing a widening gap between the pace of cyberattacks and the ability of governments and organisations to respond.

He described the first as the “attacker’s clock”, where artificial intelligence (AI) is enabling cybercriminals to launch increasingly sophisticated attacks within seconds.

 Highlighting the changing nature of cybercrime, he warned that attackers no longer necessarily need to deploy malicious software to compromise systems, with stolen credentials and AI-generated impersonations providing alternative means of gaining access. 

Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe was the Guest of Honour at the Summit held at Cinnamon Grand, Colombo drawing nearly 400 participants. 

“Scams are becoming the digital pandemic of our time. AI-enabled attacks are accelerating at an alarming pace, with attackers reportedly operating in as little as 16 seconds and their activity increasing by 89% in a single year. They no longer need sophisticated malware. They don’t break in. They simply log in using stolen passwords or AI-generated voices that sound just like your CEO,” Eng. Weeraratne said.

The second, the “quantum clock”, represents the longer-term threat posed by advances in quantum computing to widely used encryption technologies. Eng. Weeraratne cautioned that organisations must prepare for a future in which sufficiently powerful quantum computers could compromise existing cryptographic protections, potentially exposing sensitive information collected by attackers today.

Referring to international efforts to develop quantum-resistant encryption, he urged institutions to assess their existing cryptographic systems and establish transition plans before current technologies become vulnerable.

However, he identified the third, the “trust clock”, as particularly critical to Sri Lanka’s digital transformation ambitions. “The third clock is the trust clock. It moves slowly, but it is the least forgiving of all. Trust takes years to build, yet it can be shattered in seconds. For Sri Lanka, the challenge is twofold: accelerating digital transformation while ensuring that every cyber incident does not undermine the public confidence we are working so hard to build,” he stressed.

The Deputy Minister said Sri Lanka was confronting the dual challenge of accelerating digital adoption while protecting citizens from increasingly frequent cyber incidents. He warned that inadequate cybersecurity protections could discourage individuals from embracing digital payments and online services, undermining efforts to build a competitive digital economy.

Against this backdrop, Eng. Weeraratne outlined several Government initiatives aimed at strengthening Sri Lanka’s national cybersecurity architecture.

Central to these efforts is the proposed Cybersecurity Bill, which would establish a Cybersecurity Regulatory Authority empowered to introduce and enforce cybersecurity standards across public and private sector institutions. He explained that the Sri Lanka Computer Emergency Readiness Team (CERT) currently functions primarily as an incident-response organisation and lacks comprehensive regulatory powers to mandate cybersecurity compliance.

The proposed authority would address this gap by establishing enforceable requirements to improve institutional preparedness and strengthen protection against cyber threats.

The Government is also working towards establishing a Defence Cyber Command to strengthen national security capabilities against large-scale cyberattacks. Eng. Weeraratne emphasised that cybersecurity incidents affecting essential infrastructure could rapidly escalate into national security emergencies, requiring coordinated defensive capabilities beyond conventional incident-response mechanisms.

Another key initiative involves establishing permanent cybersecurity monitoring capabilities, including a National Cybersecurity Operations Centre, to provide round-the-clock oversight of connected Government digital systems. He said these measures would be complemented by efforts to consolidate scattered Government data into a smaller number of highly secured cloud platforms.

Highlighting the scale of domestic cybersecurity challenges, Eng. Weeraratne pointed out that the Sri Lanka CERT received more than 12,600 complaints during 2025, averaging approximately 35 daily. He also referred to law enforcement operations targeting foreign nationals allegedly involved in cyber-enabled scam activities in Sri Lanka, describing the global expansion of digital fraud as an increasingly serious security concern.

However, the Deputy Minister stressed that Government intervention alone would be insufficient to address the three cybersecurity challenges.

He called on corporate boards to review their cybersecurity preparedness at least quarterly, ensuring that technology teams receive the resources and institutional support necessary to manage emerging threats. Organisations must also inventory their cryptographic systems, plan their transition towards quantum-resistant technologies, and strengthen employee cybersecurity awareness, he said. Warning that a single employee mistake could compromise even highly secured systems, Eng. Weeraratne emphasised the importance of continuous staff training alongside technological safeguards.

“The Government cannot tackle these emerging cybersecurity threats alone. The private sector must take greater responsibility, with cybersecurity readiness reviewed at board level at least quarterly. This will ensure that IT teams receive the necessary support and resources to identify and mitigate risks. At the same time, every institution must assess its existing cryptographic systems and develop a clear transition plan towards quantum-resistant technologies. Cybersecurity must become a strategic priority at the highest level of every organisation,” emphasised Eng. Weeraratne.

title: Digital microlenders run riot in ’regulatory black hole’ | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:24
-     - 88

Digital microloan providers operate in a 'regulatory black hole' that has let misleading advertising, hidden charges, and abusive debt collection go unchecked, a new study has found.

In its report ‘In the Shadows of Fast Credit: Examining Digital Micro Lending in Sri Lanka,’ released last week, Colombo-based think tank Centre for a Smart Future (CSF) said these lenders fall outside the direct scope of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL), which regulates only deposit-taking institutions. 

The Microfinance and Credit Regulatory Authority Act, passed in March, covers digital lending, but the Authority has yet to be established and the Act is reportedly being amended.

Authored by Piyumi Wattuhewa and Iromi Perera, the study combined 39 borrower interviews across the island with a review of seven prominent services: LotusLoan, CashX, OnCredit, Monigo, Fino, Loanme, and LoanPlus.

Advertisements promise up to Rs. 200,000 within five minutes, up to Rs. 40,000 at '0% interest', no documentation, and instant approval, often timed to long weekends and major holidays. The costs sit in the fine print. Only OnCredit's terms and conditions mention a late fee of 2.5% a day, while Fino, Monigo and Loanme charge 10% of the unpaid principal every few days after the due date. Borrowers reported paying Rs. 4,500 in interest on a Rs. 9,000 loan and a Rs. 3,500 service fee on a Rs. 5,000 loan. One borrower with a Rs. 300 shortfall was told a year later that more than Rs. 100,000 was due after interest had been added.

"Sometimes I wonder if they are charging interest at their discretion," another borrower said.

Terms are hard to reach and harder to contest. Only one of the seven websites offered Tamil and only two had Sinhala terms and conditions. OnCredit can extend overdue loans potentially an unlimited number of times, LoanPlus terms authorise direct withdrawals from borrowers' bank accounts without further permission, and some terms prevent borrowers from taking disputes to court.

Collection practices drew the gravest findings. Agents contacted borrowers' friends, relatives, employers and children's teachers, threatened guarantors, circulated false claims of extramarital affairs, and warned of lawsuits, Police involvement, and home visits.

"I received about 50 to 60 phone calls a day threatening me into repaying the money," one borrower said.

One woman said she had decided to take her own life before her family intervened. Others reported depression, strained marriages, and closed businesses. Many borrowed from one service to repay another.

"Taking loans from these companies is like holding a tiger by its tail," said a woman who fell into such a debt trap after her husband, a day labourer, could not work through prolonged rain.

Data privacy is a further concern. All seven apps collect personal information, more than half request access to photo galleries, files, and financial information, and one requests contact list access. People on borrowers' contact lists were reportedly called during repayment delays. Only one service specified a data retention period. The authors argue these practices may conflict with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), whose substantial provisions are reported to take effect on 1 January 2027.

The services are interconnected and foreign-linked. OnCredit is linked to SpaceCrew Finance in Kyiv and Fino is part of Latvia's Sun Finance Group. The developers of all seven are members of the Digital Alternative Lending Association (DALA), which describes itself as the only self-regulatory body for digital lending. Its current Directors are from Portugal, Latvia, and Russia.

Yet the demand is real. Borrowers, including daily-wage earners, business owners, teachers, and homemakers, took more than half of the loans for sudden expenses such as illness and about 15% to repay other debts, finding banks too slow, document-heavy, or reliant on collateral.

"By the time we get the loan from the bank, the patient is already dead," one respondent said.

Under Section 37, the Act would allow regulation of interest, fees, recovery practices, and complaint handling, but the Government is considering revising it later this year, which could delay implementation.

CSF called for the Act to be fast-tracked with digital lending explicitly in scope, and for a framework regulating fees, interest rates, recovery practices, and loan disclosure. It urged sector-specific data protection rules before PDPA enforcement, clearer responsibilities for cyber harassment, oversight of misleading advertisements, stronger social protection, and community-based credit with transparent terms.

Anyone in distress can call CCCline at 1333, a 24/7, confidential and toll-free crisis support service, or the National Mental Health Helpline at 1926.

title: Sri Lanka’s Rs. 1.5 b interim digital and PR push gathers pace despite delays | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:23
-     - 88

By Charumini de Silva

Sri Lanka’s Rs. 1.5 billion interim tourism promotion drive is moving into execution across key international markets despite delays, with campaigns in the UK and Germany now awarded and three other markets still progressing through the procurement process.

“The synchronised eight-month digital and public relations (PR) campaigns in the UK and Germany are set to roll out, with the first German market production scheduled for release next week,” Sri Lanka Tourism Promotion Bureau (SLTPB) Managing Director Sanjaya Niroshan told 

the Daily FT.

The campaigns, originally scheduled for September, were strategically aligned with major international travel trade platforms including the WTM in London, which was missed this year, and the ITB Berlin to strengthen Sri Lanka’s visibility among travellers and industry stakeholders in two of its key European source markets.

Each campaign carries a budget of Rs. 100 million and will focus on destination repositioning through influencer engagement, trade promotions, and targeted digital media buying.

As per the SLTPB’s strategy, the overall interim program will span six priority source markets including Australia, UK, Germany, India, China, and Russia from August 2026 to April 2027, with France, Italy, Spain, the Middle East, Scandinavia, Poland, Japan, South Korea to follow. However, given the geopolitical uncertainties in some of the markets, new markets have been considered.

“The procurement process for the seven-month digital and PR activations for India, China, and Russia is now in its final stage,” he confirmed, adding that the Bureau is planning to start awarding contracts for France, Vietnam, and Korea markets immediately after.

The original rollout schedule envisaged the China and Russia campaigns commencing in September and the Indian campaign in October 2026, which reflects the slippage in the execution timetable.

The SLTPB Managing Director said the first phase covering Australia has been underway since August and is scheduled to continue till February 2027. “The Australian campaign served as the initial operational proof point, incorporating digital activations and trade roadshows across Melbourne, Sydney, Perth, and Adelaide,” he added. 

The overall interim strategy is designed to maintain a sustained international marketing presence rather than relying on fragmented short-term advertising bursts. The Bureau’s broader objectives are to generate arrivals to support hotel occupancy and employment, increase daily visitor spending, extend tourism activity into underdeveloped destinations, particularly in the Northern and Eastern provinces, and diversify the country’s tourism offering beyond traditional sun-and-sand experiences.

The blueprint unveiled in August 2026 follows a four-stage conversion approach of identifying target traveller segments, prioritising tourism products, mapping destinations that deliver those experiences, and developing compelling content to convert interest into bookings. The product mix spans leisure, culture, nature, adventure, wellness, luxury, and MICE (Meetings, Incentives, Conferences and Exhibitions).

For execution, the SLTPB has appointed a production agency for campaign films and digital and PR agencies for Australia, the UK, and Germany. Its digital partnerships include Meta and TikTok through authorised sales partners, and Roar Global and YouTube through Aleph Holdings and Yandex for search coverage across Russia and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).

The Market Development Facility (MDF) funded by the Australian Government is supporting local agency oversight, training and development campaign monitoring, and evaluation, while the Digital Marketing Association of Sri Lanka (DMASL) is assisting with campaign optimisation and capacity building.

The digital strategy also seeks to strengthen Sri Lanka’s visibility across emerging travel discovery channels, including artificial intelligence (AI) assistance, generative chatbots, and short-form video platforms, through improved destination data and regional itinerary content.

title: CBSL tightens checks on $ 50,000 import advances after repeated abuse | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:22
-     - 259

CBSL Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) has tightened controls on import advance payments after detecting repeated abuse of a facility that allowed importers to remit up to $ 50,000 abroad against an invoice without the goods ever arriving, Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe said on Friday.

Speaking at the post-Monetary Policy Review media briefing, Dr. Weerasinghe said the CBSL’s Department of Foreign Exchange was investigating outflows made under an earlier circular issued by the Import and Export Control Department. He said ‘the number of unnotified cases was massive’ and that action had so far been taken only on the cases that had been reported.

Under the earlier rules, an importer could obtain an advance of up to $ 50,000 from a commercial bank by presenting an invoice. The payment was recorded in the Customs ASYCUDA system, and the goods were required to arrive within 180 days. Because banks released funds against an invoice and non-arrival could only be confirmed after 180 days, abuse could go undetected for months.

Dr. Weerasinghe said checks had found that ‘the very same person had come to certain bank branches representing different companies’ to obtain repeated advances.

Customs was required to notify the CBSL’s Foreign Exchange Department when goods failed to arrive, but had not shared this information for a long period despite repeated requests. Some transactions were never recorded at Customs at all. Customs has previously said the alleged transfers fell outside its operational mandate, and that such transactions would have been visible to the banking system and the CBSL’s Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU).

Applicants must now provide a Tax Identification Number (TIN) to request an advance. The Import and Export Control Department has issued regulations requiring background checks before funds are released, covering whether the importer has prior records, who the beneficial owner is, and what the company does. A new mechanism also allows commercial banks to check whether an applicant has already obtained an advance from another bank.

Fines have been imposed on a large number of companies. The cases are being treated as fraud, with legal action being pursued alongside regulatory penalties, following a Police investigation prompted by information that individuals were using the facility repeatedly.

Violations by Board of Investment (BOI)-registered companies are handled by the Import and Export Control Department, while the CBSL’s Foreign Exchange Department acts against other entities once Customs reports them.

The measures add to regulations gazetted on 18 June under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, which require banks to report import-related foreign currency payments to Customs in real time and importers to register with Customs before making advance payments. Those rules followed investigations into more than $ 85 million in alleged remittances for imports that never entered the country.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake told Parliament in June that nearly $ 1 billion had been remitted through bank telegraphic transfers as advance payments since 2023 without any imports arriving. He linked the transactions to drug money and criminal activity, alleging the involvement of certain bank branches.

CBSL officials later told Parliament’s Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) that the FIU had repeatedly warned successive governments, the Treasury, and banks from 2021 that advance import payments were being used for trade-based money laundering.

title: Heritance Ahungalla celebrates 45 years of architectural legacy with ‘45 to Infinity’ | Daily FT

The Heritance Ahungalla marks its 45th anniversary on 23 November 2026 with ‘45 to Infinity’, a celebration honouring the architectural legacy of Geoffrey Bawa, the people who have shaped the property’s journey and its enduring place in Sri Lanka’s hospitality landscape. 

More than a milestone, the anniversary reflects four and a half decades of evolution, during which the property has remained deeply connected to its natural surroundings and architectural identity.

Originally opened in 1981 as the Triton Hotel, Heritance Ahungalla was conceived as a distinctive coastal retreat by Geoffrey Bawa, Sri Lanka’s pioneering architect and a leading figure of Tropical Modernism. At a time when resort design often placed buildings at the centre of the experience, Bawa envisioned a property that embraced its environment, allowing the ocean, tropical gardens, natural light and coastal breezes to shape its character.

One of the most defining expressions of this vision is the property’s iconic infinity pool, designed to create a seamless visual connection between the pool, the Indian Ocean and the sky. Its disappearing edge captures Bawa’s philosophy of dissolving the boundaries between architecture and nature, an experience that remains as striking today as it was when the hotel first opened. The anniversary theme, ‘45 to Infinity’, draws inspiration from this architectural landmark, connecting the property’s 45-year heritage with an endless horizon of possibilities.

Throughout Heritance Ahungalla, Geoffrey Bawa’s design philosophy can be discovered across 21 distinctive architectural features. From the iconic Triton sculpture and the 600-foot Sakman Maluwa pathway to the open-air lobby, the Mirror Lounge, the 03 Blues infinity pool and carefully framed ocean views, these architectural details tell a story of harmony between nature, culture and design. Natural materials, open spaces, tropical landscaping, reflecting pools and the interplay of light and shadow create an environment where architecture and landscape exist as one.

The property’s architectural significance extends beyond its visual appeal. It represents an important chapter in Sri Lanka’s design heritage and continues to attract guests, architects and design enthusiasts eager to experience Bawa’s approach to Tropical Modernism. Through its anniversary celebrations, Heritance Ahungalla will bring this legacy to life with architectural storytelling, guided experiences and a dedicated content series exploring the distinctive design elements found throughout the property.

Beyond its architecture, the story of Heritance Ahungalla is equally one of people, relationships and shared experiences. Over the past 45 years, the property has welcomed generations of travellers, celebrated personal milestones and offered individuals the opportunity to build lasting careers in hospitality. Its team members, including those who have dedicated decades of service to the hotel, remain an integral part of its identity.

Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings PLC Chairperson Stasshani Jayawardena said: “Heritance Ahungalla represents an important part of Sri Lanka’s architectural and hospitality heritage. For 45 years, it has stood as a testament to Geoffrey Bawa’s remarkable vision and to the enduring value of creating experiences that are deeply connected to their surroundings. This milestone is also an opportunity to recognise the generations of dedicated team members, guests and partners who have contributed to its journey. As we celebrate this legacy, we remain committed to preserving its distinctive identity while looking towards the opportunities that lie ahead.”

Aitken Spence Hotel Holdings PLC Managing Director Susith Jayawickrama said: “The 45-year journey of Heritance Ahungalla is a story of vision, resilience and the people who have brought that vision to life. From its beginnings as the Triton Hotel to its continued recognition as a landmark of Geoffrey Bawa’s architectural philosophy, the property has maintained a distinctive place within Sri Lanka’s hospitality landscape. As we mark this anniversary, we extend our appreciation to our teams, guests and partners who have been part of this journey. The ‘45 to Infinity’ campaign reflects our commitment to honouring this remarkable heritage while continuing to create meaningful experiences for generations to come.”

title: Illicit cigarettes cost Rs. 29.5 b in lost taxes in 2025: Oxford Economics | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:00
-     - 34

Illicit cigarettes cost the Government an estimated Rs. 29.5 billion in lost tax revenue in 2025, equal to 17% of the legal industry’s direct tax contribution, even as the illicit share of the market fell to 20%, according to a report by Oxford Economics commissioned by Ceylon Tobacco Company PLC (CTC).

The report, ‘The Economic Impact of the Cigarette Industry in Sri Lanka’, estimates the loss at Rs. 24.6 billion in sales taxes, comprising Rs. 18.6 billion in excise duty, Rs. 5.4 billion in Value Added Tax (VAT), and Rs. 600 million in Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL), plus Rs. 4.9 billion in corporate and labour income taxes. Had illicit products been unavailable, smokers would have bought an extra 303 million duty-paid cigarettes, the report said, based on what illicit smokers told a survey they would switch to.

Illicit Factory Made Cigarettes (FMC), mostly smuggled into the country, accounted for an estimated 470 million sticks, or 20% of FMC consumption, in 2025, down from a peak of 32% in 2024, according to research by consultancy PepperCube. The illicit share stood at 15% in 2018, when it first emerged as a significant problem. The report attributed the decline to a sharp increase in illicit cigarette prices and a growing number of retailers unwilling to stock them due to Government enforcement, as well as a more moderate 5.9% excise increase in 2025, after hikes of 44% in 2023 and 14% in 2024.

The PepperCube survey of almost 11,500 male smokers aged 22-64 found 11.5% consumed illicit cigarettes, with prevalence exceeding 20% in several districts and particularly high in Batticaloa, Puttalam, and Ratnapura. Almost half of illicit smokers cited affordability as a reason. Over 2016-2025, consumer prices rose by 140%, while prices of tier 1 cigarettes rose by about 350% and tier 4 by about 250%, driven by above-inflation excise increases. Legal cigarette consumption halved to 1.9 billion sticks from 3.9 billion over the period.

“Continued efforts to reduce illicit trade could, therefore, help protect an important source of Government revenue,” the report said.

The legal FMC value chain contributed an estimated Rs. 181 billion in taxes in 2025, equal to 3.6% of all Government tax revenue. CTC’s own contribution was Rs. 177 billion, including Rs. 112 billion in excise duty, Rs. 33.4 billion in VAT, Rs. 24.7 billion in corporate tax, Rs. 3.7 billion in SSCL, and Rs. 3.2 billion in Withholding Tax on dividends. Taxes accounted for 82% of the average retail price of cigarettes. The report noted corporate tax on the sector was raised to 45% from 40% in 2024, which it described as one of the highest rates in the world for the tobacco sector.

Cigarette-related sales taxes accounted for 2.7% of Sri Lanka’s total tax and non-tax revenue, against 1.8% in Pakistan, 1.4% in India, and a global median of 1%, based on World Health Organisation 

(WHO) data.

The report said this revenue matters given the fiscal outlook. The Budget deficit narrowed to 2.3% of GDP in 2025 from 11.7% in 2021, but Oxford Economics projects it to widen to 5.2% in 2026 and 5.8% in 2027, following Cyclone Ditwah in late 2025 and the early 2026 Middle East conflict. “Against this background, an unexpected decline in cigarette-related revenues could make fiscal consolidation more difficult,” it said.

Beedi, hand-rolled tobacco wrapped in tendu leaf, poses a larger challenge to the tax base. Beedi consumption, legal and illicit, doubled over 2016-2025 to 6.5 billion sticks, accounting for 73% of all tobacco sticks consumed in 2025, against 22% for legal cigarettes and 6% for illicit cigarettes. Beedi attracts no excise duty as of August 2026, only a tobacco tax of Rs. 3 per stick since April 2025, up from Rs. 2 when introduced in 2023. At Rs. 10-15 a stick, beedi retails at little more than a third of the price of Capstan, the cheapest legal cigarette, with reports of widespread smuggling of beedi-related products.

“Strengthening enforcement and compliance measures could help bring beedies into the tax net and provide an additional source of revenue to the Government,” the report said.

The industry’s total contribution to GDP was estimated at Rs. 74 billion, or 0.2% of national output, comprising a direct contribution of Rs. 61.2 billion, Rs. 6.5 billion from Rs. 8.1 billion in domestic procurement, and Rs. 6.3 billion from wage-funded spending. The direct contribution is comparable to that of cereals (Rs. 59.5 billion) and rubber (Rs. 65.6 billion).

The value chain supported 81,400 jobs, or 1% of national employment. These include 62,700 jobs across 74,600 retail outlets, 14,600 leaf farmers and associated workers, 1,100 jobs in 11 distribution companies, and 301 CTC employees. CTC, the country’s sole legal cigarette manufacturer, produced 1.92 billion cigarettes in 2025 using 1.5 million kilograms of tobacco leaf sourced from 884 contracted farmers and 5,610 sub-growers.

“The analysis does not consider the broader social and health impacts of tobacco consumption, whether legal or illicit,” the report said.

title: Dayasiri questions judicial independence, warns against weaponising criminal justice system | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:01

MP Dayasiri Jayasekara

MP Dayasiri Jayasekara on Saturday in Parliament raised concerns over the independence of the judiciary and the potential misuse of criminal law against political opponents, warning that the credibility of Sri Lanka’s justice system depends on Courts retaining the authority to question the State and scrutinise the grounds for arrest and detention.

Speaking in Parliament, he, questioned provisions of the Anti-Corruption Act that require Magistrates to remand suspects upon the submission of a certificate by the Commission to Investigate Allegations of Bribery or Corruption (CIABOC) Director-General, subject to statutory conditions.

He said Section 149 of the 2023 Act gives significant weight to such certificates in determining remand, with bail being granted only in exceptional circumstances and with reasons recorded by the Magistrate. He questioned whether citizens have a meaningful opportunity to challenge the factual basis of a certificate that could result in their continued detention.

Referring to proceedings involving MP Namal Rajapaksa, he said the Fort Magistrate had sought clarification in September on whether the Director-General had submitted such a certificate in related proceedings. “Our duty in this House is to ask what opportunity any citizen has to test the factual basis of a certificate that can keep him behind bars. A Magistrate who must sign the remand order must have a meaningful opportunity to examine the grounds on which a person loses his liberty,” he stressed.

He urged the Justice Minister to disclose the number of Section 149 certificates issued annually, the duration of remand in the cases concerned, and how many had proceeded to trial, saying such information would enable Parliament to assess the practical impact of the provision without interfering in pending cases.

Jayasekara also cautioned against investigations in which individuals were allegedly targeted first, with investigators subsequently seeking offences to fit them. Such practices, he argued, undermined the presumption of innocence guaranteed under Article 13(5) of the Constitution and risked turning legal proceedings into instruments of punishment before guilt was established.

“As a lawyer and a Member of this House, I am deeply concerned about what happens to that citizen when the decision to pursue him is taken first and the search for an offence begins afterwards. An honest investigation follows the evidence, wherever it leads and whoever may be implicated. Once those in authority select a person and ask investigators to find an offence that will fit, they have already decided whom to punish. Everything that follows carries the appearance of a legal process. That is precisely what makes the abuse so dangerous,” he said.

He also questioned the Government’s decision under the 22nd Amendment to raise the retirement age of Supreme Court judges from 65 to 67 and Court of Appeal judges from 63 to 65, arguing that the revised limits could have been applied only to future appointments rather than extending the tenure of serving judges.

On the constitution of judicial benches in politically sensitive and high-profile cases, including matters relating to the proposed Protection of the State from Terrorism Bill and Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, he called for greater transparency in the exercise of the Chief Justice’s powers under Article 132.

While affirming the Chief Justice’s constitutional authority to constitute benches, Jayasekara proposed that the judiciary publish the principles governing bench assignments and maintain a public record of the benches appointed to hear cases of significant public interest. Such disclosure, he said, would help address concerns over repeated assignments of the same judges to politically sensitive cases while strengthening public confidence in the judiciary.

Drawing on Sri Lanka’s judicial history, he cited the 1937 Mark Bracegirdle case, in which Chief Justice Sir Sidney Abrahams and two other judges ordered the release of Bracegirdle after examining the legality of the colonial Governor’s deportation order. He said the episode demonstrated that even the most powerful executive authority must be required to justify the detention of an individual.

Jayasekara also warned that using the criminal justice system to prevent political opponents from contesting elections would undermine the franchise and deny voters their right to choose. 

“A Government that weaponises the criminal justice system to disqualify an opponent betrays its own lack of confidence in facing the people at the next election. If you believe you have earned a second mandate, go before the country, defend your record and ask for it. What right have you to narrow the people’s choice before a single vote has been cast?”

Drawing parallels with the 1980 decision under former President J.R. Jayewardene’s Government to strip former Prime Minister Sirimavo Bandaranaike of her civic rights, which prevented her from contesting the 1982 Presidential Election, he said the consequences extended beyond the individual to the electorate.

He recalled that Bandaranaike returned as Prime Minister for a third time in 1994, arguing that political opponents should be challenged at the ballot box rather than through the misuse of State institutions.

“Have the courage to face your opponents at the polls. Leave the choice to the people,” he told the Government benches.

He warned that the erosion of judicial independence could have a chilling effect on trade unionists, Opposition politicians, and ordinary citizens, particularly those seeking to challenge Government actions or expose wrongdoing, adding that an independent judiciary remained the last safeguard against executive overreach.

The proposed legislation is intended to replace both the Immigrants and Emigrants Act (Chapter 351) and the Passports and Exit Permits Act No. 53 of 1971, bringing the country’s immigration framework in line with contemporary international standards and technological developments.

Even taking the regular lift to the first floor was an experience in itself—the character of the building, the architecture, and the sense of history surrounding it reminded me that this was a place created in 1844, carrying with it a remarkable legacy and an ancient glory.

Early one morning, I woke up and found the roads almost completely empty. I walked towards Kandy Lake and sat on one of those simple concrete benches, looking across the water towards the Sri Dalada Maligawa. There was a slight drizzle, and the quietness of the morning created a special atmosphere.

As I sat there, I began looking carefully at the architecture surrounding the lake. Dutch, British and traditional Kandyan influences appeared to blend together in a remarkable historical landscape. I then walked across Trincomalee Street and looked closely at some of the older buildings.

And I asked myself: What have we done to Kandy?

Kandy has all the ingredients of a world-class tourist destination. The Temple of the Tooth, the lake, the historic buildings, the surrounding hills, the ancient traditions and the unique cultural character of the city make it, in many ways, a natural tourist paradise.

Yet I could not help feeling that we have missed a golden opportunity to preserve and develop Kandy in the way it deserves.

My vision for Kandy would be very different. I would like to see a city where people, not vehicles, dominate the historic centre. Certain streets could be progressively closed to vehicular traffic, allowing visitors to walk, explore and experience the architecture, history and culture at a leisurely pace.

Imagine walking through the historic heart of Kandy without the constant movement of vehicles—stopping at an old building, discovering a small shop, sitting beside the lake, visiting the temples and experiencing the city rather than simply passing through it.

Modern development has its place, but it should not come at the expense of the architectural and historical character that makes Kandy unique. New construction in sensitive historic areas should be carefully controlled so that the city does not lose the very character that tourists come to experience.

Kandy should not merely be a place tourists pass through on their way to somewhere else. Kandy itself should be the destination.

With proper conservation, pedestrianisation, traffic management, restoration of historic buildings, carefully designed tourism infrastructure and a clear long-term vision, Kandy could become one of the greatest cultural tourism destinations in Sri Lanka—and potentially one of the most distinctive heritage cities in Asia.

We have the lake.

We have the Maligawa.

We have the temples.

We have the hills.

We have centuries of history.

We have the architecture.

We have the culture.

What more could a tourist paradise ask for?

What Kandy needs now is not more concrete. It needs imagination, protection, investment and, above all, a vision.

title: Why revenue dip amidst rising tourist arrivals is not necessarily a bad thing | Daily FT

Note: 2026 figure is an estimation as per the September 2026 SLTDA report

Source: CBSL

Annual tourist arrivals are expected to hit an all-time high, at 2.4 million by the end of 2026. However, the revenue numbers tell a different story. Per tourist spending has reduced dramatically. The average spending for 2026 is expected to be roughly the same.

If we pass the 2.4 million mark in 2026, it will be an all-time high.

Why is per day spending getting lower?

Methodology revised to obtain realistic estimates, which is lower

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) in its External Sector Performance Report in February 2026, mentioned how the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority has changed their estimations based on Departure Surveys. 

Now, the SLTDA takes tourist arrivals, average stay period and average spending per day into account.

They have also considered the seasonality of average stay per tourist. Therefore, average spending per day is revised from August 2025. 

These revisions will give a more accurate, rather low figure of spending than previous.

LKR/USD Exchange Rate depreciated fast and service quality dropped due to rising inflation

Therefore, fewer dollars are needed to purchase goods in Sri Lanka. The country was already grappling with many structural issues, mounting debt and the exchange rate ballooned out of control in 2022. 

As the products get ‘cheaper’ more budget travelers would opt to visit. Also, the imported goods fetch a very high price, then the quality of service begins to drop, foreign service providers, travel operators pull out their investment due to uncertainty. ‘High-end’ tourism will no longer be supported.

Informal sector leakages

Informal sector transactions are very difficult to trace the flow. Most are cash and ledger books are not maintained. No records are kept. The services do not get captured in the GDP.

Actual spending is less

What the figures say, could be the plain truth. Tourists spend less than before. The latest reports show that the inflow from Western European countries have eroded, while India and China grab the top spots in source markets. Indian tourist arrivals make the largest share, close to 30%. 

For Indian and other Asian tourists, the cultural experience, the climate and surroundings are familiar to their home country. Therefore, the spending could be mostly on key, planned visit, or pre-determined at a package rate.

However, ‘unplanned’ sporadic spending can be expected from the Western tourists, outside their basic needs, owing to the different cultural experience.

On a brighter note

The money could be actually flowing into local communities, smallholder establishments

Another view is that the tourists are opting for smaller, informal service establishments/vendors. Their transactions are off record and mostly in cash. While State Revenue may not benefit, the local value chains could be thriving on this. However, there is little data to confirm this fact.

Frequent use of QR pay is an option

If the sector needs systematic, resilient growth, promoting digital payment methods is a must. It is not always about being captured for tax purposes, but also for transparency and safety of both service providers and the tourists.

Microdata-driven analysis of service providers

Rather than solely relying on Tourists Surveys, a closer look of the characteristics of the service providers, amenities, surrounding can give a better perspective. And to cross-reference the survey data. Such a data driven exercise can give insights as to the quality of one of Sri Lanka’s main export.
