title: IPS’s State of the Economy 2026: More worm’s eye analysis than bird’s eye analysis | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:24
-     - 100

IPS ‘State of the Economy’ report is far too precious a document to be ignored by those entrusted with shaping the 

economic future of this country

Simultaneous bird’s eye and worm’s eye analyses

Those who read my previous week’s article in this newspaper, titled ‘Bird’s Eye View of the Economy: “Ok, Stable and Growing”; Worm’s Eye, “Not That Rosy”’, will find a timely companion in the newly released annual flagship report by the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS). 

This publication skillfully mirrors that dual perspective, initialising its coverage with a four-chapter macroeconomic analysis—a high-level evaluation of national economic metrics like inflation, total output, and trade balances—before guiding readers through a much grimmer reality across the remaining ten chapters. This extensive second section serves as a “worm’s-eye” analysis, focusing on microeconomic conditions to explain how individual households, small businesses, and workers are actually faring on the ground. 

Established in the late 1980s as an independent State apparatus, IPS was specifically created to provide autonomous policy advice, filling critical gaps in the less comprehensive reporting historically produced by the Central Bank and the Ministry of Finance. For nearly four decades, the institute has published this State of the Economy report every November, delivering crucial data just in time to assist the Ministry of Finance with its upcoming budget planning. 

Because the official annual economic reviews from the Central Bank and the Finance Ministry for 2026 will not see the light of day until April and June 2027, respectively, this IPS report acts as the quintessential early bird catching the worm. Crucially, the 2026 report zeroes in on structural policy choices required to achieve durable, long-term growth—a pressing challenge for Sri Lanka as the nation prepares to exit the protective shield of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and its Extended Fund Facility (EFF), a structured loan program designed to stabilise bankrupt economies, which concludes in March 2027.

Canvassing for social inclusion

In the opening chapter, titled ‘Policy Perspectives’, IPS synthesises its institutional wisdom on how Sri Lanka should craft strategic policies to sustain economic growth once the safety net of the IMF is gone. However, the report candidly admits that the State does not possess total freedom to design a completely independent policy package just yet. It explicitly notes that “growth under the guardrails is the operating reality of 2026 and will remain so for the duration of the IMF program and beyond.” This means that the strict fiscal limits and structural benchmarks agreed with international lenders will dictate national budgeting for years to come. 

Crucially, IPS reminds policymakers that an IMF program is essentially an emergency toolkit designed strictly to achieve macroeconomic stability—the stabilisation of national balances, such as curbing hyperinflation and steadying the currency. True, durable growth relies on an entirely different set of foundations. According to IPS as outlined in the State of the Economy Report for 2026, long-term economic expansion requires boosting the economy’s potential output through advanced technology, a more highly skilled workforce, and robust capital investment. It also demands careful mitigation of environmental damage, a steady elevation of living standards, and deep social inclusion—a development model ensuring that vulnerable or marginalised groups are not left behind but are given equal access to economic opportunities and fruits of economic advancement. 


Thus, the IPS rejects the outdated philosophy of chasing growth for growth’s sake. Instead, it advises the Government to balance development with the genuine wellbeing of ordinary citizens. There is ultimately little virtue in economic growth unless it preserves the environment for posterity and invites every citizen to become a partner in national prosperity. In stark contrast, any policy framework that fosters social exclusion—allowing a select elite to hoard the fruits of growth—inevitably triggers severe social, political, and economic disorder. 

Sri Lanka learnt this lesson at a catastrophic cost in 2022. On that occasion, ordinary people, pushed to the absolute brink by unendurable financial burdens, revolted against the State, culminating in the incumbent President fleeing the country under the cover of darkness and paving the way for a brand-new administration to set in. Fresh with the trauma of that hazardous memory, IPS is understandably desperate to avoid a repeat of history. It is precisely this fear of renewed instability that drives the institute to advocate for social inclusion as an indispensable goal of modern economic policy. It ends the chapter with a wise counsel in this regard. It says that Sri Lanka can and must grow, but it must grow differently to achieve its ambitious socio-economic targets.

Stagnating economy as the baseline

While Sri Lanka has undoubtedly engineered an economic recovery from the absolute nadir of the 2022 crisis, IPS explicitly warns against the danger of complacency. The nation must not get stuck savouring this initial survival; instead, it must urgently transition from mere recovery to long-term economic resilience—the structural strength required to absorb, adapt to, and withstand sudden international financial shocks without collapsing. If this deeper resilience is not built, Sri Lanka risks becoming a defenceless victim to future global crises, leaving the economy damaged beyond redemption. 

Achieving this safety net demands tough structural changes, including comprehensive tariff and labour reforms to boost competitiveness, alongside deep investment in modern infrastructure. Crucially, IPS stresses that this does not just mean pouring concrete into traditional physical projects like highways, but rather building digital infrastructure to modernise transactions, governance, and trade. National economic policies must be firmly geared toward this modernisation, yet the hurdles remain monumental. 

The report reveals a grim reality when looking at individual sectors: between 2015 and 2025, Sri Lanka’s agriculture completely stagnated, suffering a below-zero compound annual growth rate (CAGR)—a metric that measures the smoothed, steady annual growth rate of an industry over a specific period, showing that real farming output actually shrank over the decade. Over the same 10-year period, industrial growth averaged a miniscule 0.5%,while the services sector averaged just 2%. These low numbers, as revealed by IPS, contributed to a very low real economic growth over that entire decade hovering barely above zero. 

What this means is that the size of the cake that determines the real prosperity of people has remained almost the same. But when the inequitable income distribution is reckoned, the poor have become poorer, while the rich richer demonstrating the telltale signs of an exclusive economic growth. Thus, the sobering conclusion of IPS is that it is precisely from this gloomy, fragile baseline that Sri Lanka must now design its blueprint for truly durable growth.

Growth-oriented fiscal reorientation

Under the strict guidance of IMF, Sri Lanka’s fiscal policy—the way the Government manages its public taxation and spending—has focused intensely on achieving immediate fiscal stabilisation. However, IPS warns that while balancing the books is an absolute necessity to create a stable economic environment, it is not enough on its own to drive genuine national development. Instead of simply squeezing more taxes out of the economy, the institute highlights a critical need to maintain tax revenues while simultaneously rationalising, or streamlining, State spending. 

This is known as a balanced fiscal stance, an approach that carefully balances incoming revenue against outgoing expenses to ensure the Government’s financial position actively supports national progress. In contrast, the standard IMF blueprint prescribes a rigid strategy of revenue-based fiscal consolidation, which means narrowing the budget deficit purely by driving up Government income through higher taxes and duties. 

Although successive administrations have followed this tax-first strategy to the absolute letter, independent economists have heavily critiqued it, arguing that it suffocates local businesses and squeezes households. These experts echo the IPS view: Sri Lanka must instead pursue a balanced consolidation that cuts out wasteful expenditure while optimising tax revenue. The IPS report insists that this refined financial strategy must aim to build real prosperity for ordinary citizens through a growth-oriented reallocation of public money. 

This is broken down into a fivefold plan: directing State investment into highly productive economic zones, channeling significant resources into human capital development—which means upgrading the skills, health, and knowledge of the workforce through better education and healthcare services—and building physical infrastructure strong enough to withstand severe climate shocks. 

It also demands aggressive funding for technological innovation and digital transformations, alongside actions to improve productivity across every single sector. Crucially, this modern framework has absolutely no room for inflating recurrent expenditure—the everyday, ongoing costs of running the Government—such as expanding expensive fuel subsidies or maintaining a bloated, inefficient public service. These are exceptionally bold policy recommendations that challenge long-standing political habits.

Falling workforce

With this comprehensive overview complete, IPS shifts its focus to a detailed “worm’s-eye” analysis, examining the ground realities faced by ordinary households. At first glance, the data appears promising: Sri Lanka’s unemployment rate has fallen to approximately 4%, returning to the baseline observed before the 2022 economic collapse. 

However, the report warns that this figure is no reason for complacency. The drop in unemployment is not driven by the creation of new, productive jobs, but rather by a worrying trend of citizens completely leaving the labour force—the total pool of people who are either actively working or looking for work. This retreat is most alarming among women, whose participation rate has shrunk from roughly 35% in 2019 to just 30% in 2024. When fewer family members participate in the workforce, household income drops, directly damaging the overall welfare of dependents. For children, lower family income stunts parental investment in talent and skill development; for the elderly, it translates to reduced access to healthcare and a higher vulnerability to disease. 

Making matters worse, this low participation is exacerbated by a severe brain drain—the mass emigration of highly educated and skilled professionals seeking better opportunities abroad. As IPS bluntly notes, this flight has removed the country’s most mobile, skilled workers, making unskilled workers to occupy jobs which demand high levels of skills. At the same time, a collapse in the supply of skilled workers needed by the information and communications technology (ICT) and professional service sectors has pushed those industries to hire less qualified workers to fill the vacancies. The result of this unwarranted development is the loss of competitiveness, on one side, and low growth in productivity, on the other.

Plight of silvering people

The IPS report turns a compassionate yet analytical lens onto the plight of Sri Lanka’s rapidly ageing population, often referred to as the silvering people. While popular misconception often paints senior citizens as an economic burden who merely consume the goods produced by the younger workforce, the report vigorously corrects this bias, documenting the highly productive contributions they continue to make. In countless households, older family members look after the young, transfer invaluable traditional and professional knowledge to the next generation, and actively engage in trade and community services essential to a functioning society. Consequently, a vast market known as the silver economy has emerged around them. 


This specialised sector encompasses two main branches: silver consumption goods tailored for active older adults, and silver-care products, such as targeted healthcare and mobility aids. The IPS report emphasises that a forward-thinking economy must deliberately allocate national resources to produce these essential goods and services. 

These products are increasingly classified as age-brands, and the specialised field dedicated to developing them is formally known as gerontechnology—or more colloquially, age-tech—which uses technological solutions to improve the health, independence, and daily lives of older individuals. With Sri Lanka’s demographic shift accelerating rapidly, ensuring the wellbeing of this massive group through dedicated economic planning must become a core national priority.

A report too precious to be ignored

In my view, the IPS ‘State of the Economy’ report is far too precious a document to be ignored by those entrusted with shaping the economic future of this country. It is an indispensable roadmap, yet it suffers from one persistent, recurring vulnerability: it continues to cater almost exclusively to technically competent academics and data analysts. Not every decisionmaker, particularly within the volatile political arena, possesses the specialised training required to instantly digest its complex macroeconomic messaging and dense policy equations. 

To bridge this gap, while enthusiastically recommending this report to all policymakers, I strongly suggest that future editions should carry as addenda to them simple explanatory materials rich with easily understandable infographics—visual representations of information, data, or knowledge designed to make complex statistics quickly and easily digestible. Translating these dense chapters into scannable charts, diagrams, and visual breakdowns will democratise this vital knowledge, allowing ordinary citizens and politicians alike to fully grasp the urgent structural choices facing Sri Lanka.

My final recommendation is to Parliamentarians: Study this report from cover to cover, and if necessary, get IPS experts to explain complex matters they have presented, and use it productively for policymaking. Otherwise, it will simply remain a report, as it has happened in the past, consumed only by technical experts.  

(The writer, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, can be reached at waw1949@gmail.com)

title: A decade after Paris Agreement: Financing farms and natural capital | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:22
-     - 41

Sri Lanka should use climate finance to protect farms and the soils, water, forests and biodiversity that sustain them. A decade after the Paris Agreement entered into force, success should be judged by whether investment reduces crop losses, secures water and protects livelihoods. Farmers need timely advice as rainfall becomes less predictable; families need reliable food supplies at affordable prices.

Adopted in December 2015, opened for signature in April 2016 and brought into force in November that year, the Agreement created a shared framework to limit warming, strengthen adaptation and support developing countries. It seeks to keep warming well below 2°C while pursuing efforts towards 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. Its anniversary invites scrutiny of both achievements and unfinished work.

Progress with a widening delivery gap

The Paris Agreement established a continuing process through which countries submit climate commitments, strengthen them over time and report progress. These Nationally Determined Contributions, or NDCs, have brought climate concerns into national planning. Common reporting arrangements and periodic global reviews allow countries’ collective progress to be assessed.

Yet these institutional achievements have not secured a safe climate pathway. The Emissions Gap Report (2026) of the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) estimates that delivering national commitments and continuing similar efforts would limit warming this century to about 2.6°C. The Paris Agreement has organised the global response, but commitments and implementation remain inadequate. The Adaptation Gap Report (2025) of UNEP has estimated the annual adaptation needs for developing countries in 2035 would cost around  

$ 310–365 billion, compared with international public adaptation finance of $ 26 billion in 2023. Although the years differ, the figures illustrate the scale of the financing challenge.

According to the OECD, developed countries first exceeded their collective annual $ 100 billion climate finance goal in 2022, two years late. The 29th UNFCCC climate conference (COP29) agreed on a new goal of at least $ 300 billion annually by 2035 for developing countries. Developed countries are to lead in mobilising this finance from public, private and other sources. This is a future funding goal, not money already disbursed to vulnerable communities.

Spending priorities matter too. Reducing emissions, or mitigation, must proceed alongside adaptation that helps people cope with changing conditions. Farmers need support before harvests fail. Governments and funding agencies should assess projects by timely disbursement, lasting benefits and the share reaching those facing the greatest risks.

Sri Lanka needs results that farmers can recognise

Difficulties in the agricultural sector have emanated due to several causes, for example: Input costs, policy decisions, markets and land degradation interact with weather. Hence, attributing every production decline to climate change would weaken the argument. Finance should address demonstrated climate risks while improving farmers’ ability to respond.

The NDC 3.0 of Sri Lanka covers the period 2026–2035 and includes agriculture in both mitigation and adaptation segments. Priorities include climate advice, resilient varieties and breeds, better soil and water management, efficient input use and reduced postharvest losses. These provide a direction for investment.

There is practical experience to build on. The Green Climate Fund (GCF)-supported Climate Resilient Integrated Water Management Project connects village irrigation improvements with water security in the Malwathu Oya, Mi Oya and Yan Oya basins. This approach links farming with the landscapes supplying its water. Its lasting value requires independently verified outcomes and continued maintenance.

National commitments alone do not demonstrate greater resilience. Government agencies and project implementers should establish whether households experience fewer losses, more dependable water and more stable incomes. Interventions must remain affordable and effective after external funding ends, with clear responsibilities and national budgets for continued operation.

Make natural capital assessment a guide for investment

The Government should make natural capital assessment part of agricultural and climate investment planning. Natural capital comprises soils, water, forests, wetlands and biodiversity. These assets support farming through water regulation, erosion control and pollination. Assessing their condition helps identify where degradation threatens production and where protection offers lasting benefits.

Such assessments should identify the assets, their condition, the people who depend on them and their exposure to climate risks. Existing surveys, satellite information and local knowledge need field verification. Priority assessment areas could include upper watersheds supplying reservoirs, degraded agricultural slopes and vulnerable tank catchments.

Natural capital assessment should begin with physical measures such as soil loss, water quality, habitat condition and seasonal water availability. Economic valuation can then estimate selected benefits, including avoided sediment removal or crop losses, while explaining uncertainty. Ecological and cultural importance cannot always be expressed in rupees; valuation should not imply that every ecosystem is replaceable.

These findings should guide restoration budgets and project selection. Where erosion threatens a reservoir and nearby farms, for example, agencies could finance slope protection, streamside vegetation and improved farming practices together. Monitoring water quality and sediment would help establish whether the investment protects both agricultural production and downstream water supplies.

Conservation costs and benefits must also be shared fairly. Upstream farmers may benefit from healthier soils while bearing costs for land management changes that also help downstream water users. Technical support or payments for verified stewardship could make participation affordable. Assessments can inform contributions from public agencies, utilities and businesses, with clear land rights and benefit-sharing arrangements.

Over time, natural capital accounts could track changes in these assets alongside economic indicators. The findings should inform budgets, land-use decisions and lending. Assessments deliver value when they lead to action and subsequent monitoring.

Prioritise water and soil

The Government should prioritise reliable water management from upper catchments to farms in its climate investment program. Rehabilitating a tank without protecting its catchment leaves it exposed to sedimentation. Programs should connect watershed restoration, tank cascades, irrigation scheduling, drainage and maintenance, with farmers involved in water allocation.

Soil protection belongs in the same package. Suitable contour measures, ground cover, organic matter management and appropriate nutrient use can protect productive land. Evidence on erosion, water stress and livelihoods should guide site selection. Success should reflect soil condition, water reliability and production stability, alongside hectares treated.

Solar-powered irrigation pumps need similar care. Cleaner energy can reduce operating costs, but cheaper pumping may encourage excessive groundwater extraction. Financing should include water budgets, extraction controls and equipment maintenance.

Turn climate information into farm decisions

Forecasts must explain what expected rainfall and temperatures mean for planting, irrigation, fertiliser application and harvesting in each locality. Advice should arrive in time, in accessible languages, through trusted extension services and digital channels.

Funding should connect weather observations, soil information, field trials and farmer feedback to produce practical advice. Research on heat- and drought-tolerant varieties must connect with seed multiplication and distribution. Diversified cropping, homegardens and integrated crop–livestock systems deserve support where resources and markets are suitable. Public investment must cover extension staff and operating costs as well as equipment.

Insurance can complement these measures if farmers understand premiums, exclusions and payment rules. Weather-based products must be tested against actual losses, reducing the risk that a damaged crop receives no compensation because a distant gauge recorded different conditions.

Finance efficient production and safer harvests

Finance should support food production with fewer avoidable losses and lower environmental costs. Better fertiliser timing and placement, soil testing and integrated pest management need practical training and evidence of farm benefits. Suitable paddy water management can reduce methane emissions, provided irrigation is controllable and yields are safeguarded.

Investment should extend along the value chain. Appropriate drying, storage, packhouses, transport and efficient cooling can protect food quality and earnings. Projects need a clear climate benefit, sufficient produce and affordable operation. Otherwise, even a modern cold room may become an expensive idle asset.

Choose finance that lasts

Financing must match the investment. Grants and public budgets suit shared services such as climate information and catchment protection. Affordable loans, guarantees and private investment may suit viable storage, processing and renewable energy businesses. Smallholders should not face unaffordable debt for investments whose benefits extend across society.

The Government should develop an investment program, coordinated by the Ministry of Finance, linking agricultural resilience with natural capital protection. Each proposal needs a climate rationale, baseline, responsible institution, maintenance budget and measurable outcomes. Farmers, including women and tenants, should help design access arrangements. Implementing agencies should disclose expenditure, beneficiaries and results, provide a complaints process and commission independent evaluation. Universities can help establish baselines and assess outcomes.

Priority should be investments that farmers can sustain and public agencies can maintain. Connecting resilient farming with healthy watersheds and soils would give climate commitments practical meaning: more dependable harvests, secure livelihoods and reliable food supplies.

(The author is Senior Professor in Crop Science, Faculty of Agriculture, University of Peradeniya, Sri Lanka)

title: Budget 2027’s enhanced capital allowance: A 200% promise needs 100% clarity | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:21
-     - 96

President and Finance Minister Anura Kumara Dissanayake

Budget 2027 offers enterprises approved by the Board of Investment (BOI) an enhanced capital allowance of 200% for investing at least $ 3 million in export-oriented manufacturing or tourism development. The stated aim is to encourage private investment, promote export-oriented manufacturing and strengthen tourism. The Budget also sets itself a welcome test: every tax concession will be assessed on the economic and social benefits it generates.

The direction is right. An allowance tied to capital actually spent rewards investment that has actually happened. But read alongside the Inland Revenue Act, No. 24 of 2017 (IRA) and its latest amendment, the proposal raises a basic question that the Budget leaves unanswered: who exactly is this incentive meant to help? The answer will be found not in the Budget Speech, but in the drafting of the law.

The current framework

Section 16 of the IRA is the gateway. Capital allowances are granted on depreciable assets and computed under the Second, Fourth or Sixth Schedule. They must be claimed in the year they arise and cannot be deferred.

General capital allowance. The Fourth Schedule provides allowances on a straight-line basis for depreciable assets owned and used in the production of income. Plant, machinery, computers, vehicles and furniture are written off over five years; buildings over twenty years, at 5% a year.

The IRA defines a depreciable asset as one that:

(a) is employed in the production of income from a business and is likely to lose value because of wear and tear, obsolescence or the passing of time; but

(b) excludes goodwill, an interest in land, a membership interest in an entity and trading stock.

Temporary concession. The Sixth Schedule, read with section 201, once granted an enhanced allowance of 100% (200% in the Northern Province) on up to $ 3 million spent on buildings and fixed plant, over and above the general allowance. Even that concession excluded the expansion of an existing business, and by its own terms it expired six years after it took effect.

Enhanced capital allowance (ECA). That leaves the Second Schedule as the principal ECA regime. A person who makes a new investment in Sri Lanka is granted an allowance computed on expenses incurred on depreciable assets, other than intangibles, in addition to the general allowance. Expansions of an existing business qualify only under a BOI agreement and with specific BOI approval. The tiers are summarised below.

What Budget 2027 proposes

Technical Note 1.2 to the Budget allows BOI-approved enterprises investing at least $ 3 million in export-oriented manufacturing or tourism development to opt for an enhanced allowance of 200% of qualifying capital expenditure.  In the case of manufacturing and tourism (other than hotels), investment should be made within 3 years. For hotels, investment should be made within 5 years. An enterprise that opts in forgoes both the general allowance under the Fourth Schedule and the ECA under the Second Schedule.

New undertaking or expansion: The threshold question

The first question the law must answer is whether the 200% is for new projects, expansions, or both. The Budget refers simply to “enterprises operating under agreements with the BOI”, which on its face includes existing BOI factories and hotels. At post-Budget seminars, however, officials indicated that the intention is to cover new undertakings. If that is the policy, it must be written into the law, because the consequences for existing businesses are significant.

Under the current Second Schedule, an existing company is already at a disadvantage. The $ 250,000 tier introduced in 2026 is confined to new undertakings. An existing BOI exporter expanding by $ 2.9 million therefore receives no ECA at all, while a newly formed undertakings investing

$ 300,000 receives 100%. A company without a BOI agreement receives nothing on an expansion of any size. In effect, unless an existing business invests more than $ 3 million in depreciable assets under a specifically approved BOI expansion, there is no investment incentive.

If the proposed 200% is also confined to new undertakings, the gap widens. Businesses with an established track record, existing markets and the balance sheet to invest are left with the general allowance, while incentives flow to new entities. That is the reverse of what an investment-led recovery needs.

It also raises a question about the policy maker’s choice of words. If the shift from “investment in depreciable assets” to “qualifying capital expenditure” was intended to bring the refurbishment and modernisation of existing hotels and factories within the incentive, that intention sits uneasily with a scheme confined to new undertakings. A new undertaking has nothing to refurbish. Both cannot be true: either the wider base is meant to reach existing businesses, in which case the law must say so, or the incentive is for new undertakings only, in which case the change in wording does little for the hotels and factories that most need to reinvest.

The refurbishment gap

The issue is sharpest in tourism. Much of what existing hotels need to spend today is on refurbishment: upgrading rooms, renewing interiors and restoring properties damaged by the recent cyclone. None of this qualifies for ECA. The Act excludes the replacement of an existing depreciable asset from the definition of “expansion”, and an existing hotel is not a new undertaking. Refurbishment spending is instead relieved in one of three ways, depending on its nature.

First, repairs and maintenance that restore an asset to its original condition, including much cyclone damage, are deductible in full in the year under section 14, provided they meet the production-of-income test in section 11(1). Second, improvements, being additions or alterations that enhance the value of an asset, are also deductible under section 14 even if capital in nature. Since 1 April 2021, however, the annual deduction is capped at 5% of the written down value at the end of the previous year for buildings and 20% for other assets. The excess is added to the depreciation basis of the asset, where the written down value is nil, the improvement is deducted over twelve years for buildings and three years for other assets. Third, new furniture, fittings and equipment bought to replace old items are new depreciable assets, written off under the Fourth Schedule.

A hotel refurbishment is therefore not left without relief, but that relief is limited to 100% of cost and, for structural improvements to an older building, can take well over a decade to recover. The real gap is not repairs, which are deducted immediately, nor loose equipment, written off in five years. It is capital improvements to hotel buildings. If qualifying capital expenditure were defined to include such improvements, a 200% allowance would bring the relief forward and double it, a gain in both timing and quantum.

If the objective is to strengthen the tourism sector, as the Budget states, a well-defined refurbishment window for existing hotels, with a minimum spend, a defined completion period and a clawback, may deliver faster and more visible results than incentives for new projects alone.

“Qualifying capital expenditure”: A wider base, or a new label?

The Second Schedule allowance is anchored to depreciable assets within the Fourth Schedule classes. The Budget instead proposes 200% of “qualifying capital expenditure”, a term found nowhere in the Act. Capital expenditure is a wider concept, capable of reaching land development, lease premiums, pre-operational costs and intangibles.

If the term is defined broadly, the proposal becomes a genuine enhancement. If it is defined as expenditure on depreciable assets, it largely repeats the Second Schedule under a new label. The choice also has mechanical consequences. The Fourth Schedule rules on written down value, and on taxing the full sale proceeds of assets that received ECA, operate only on depreciable assets. They will not work on expenditure that is not attached to an asset unless the law says how.

Does 200% deliver more?

On a like-for-like base, the headline is less dramatic than it appears. A new manufacturer investing $ 10 million in depreciable assets outside the Northern Province already receives a 100% ECA plus the general allowance, adding up to around 200% of cost over time. A proposed 200% allowance in place of both delivers broadly the same total. The real gain is in timing.

That gain is clearest for new hotels, which invest mainly in buildings written off over twenty years; a front-loaded 200% would bring much of that relief forward. For manufacturers, whose plant is already written off over five years, the benefit is modest.

For new projects above $ 100 million, or in the Northern Province, current law already gives 150% or 200% plus the general allowance. “200% in place of everything” would leave these investors worse off, which is presumably why the allowance is optional. But investors can only exercise an option they can price, and they cannot price it until the law is written. Meanwhile, existing exporters expanding below $3 million, existing hotels refurbishing and non-BOI companies sit outside the frame entirely, unless the law is drafted to include them.

The global minimum tax

Any new incentive must today also be tested against the OECD/G20 BEPS framework, in particular Pillar Two, the 15% global minimum tax on large multinational groups. How a 200% allowance would interact with the minimum tax, the OECD’s new safe harbour for substance-based incentives and the case for a domestic minimum top-up tax deserve careful study before the law is finalised. They merit an article of their own. The focus here is narrower: how the Budget proposal should be embedded in the Inland Revenue Act.

Questions that need to be addressed in drafting the law

1. New undertakings, expansions, or both? The law must say so expressly, and state whether the existing Second Schedule definitions of “new undertaking” and “expansion” apply.

2. Will refurbishment count? Given the exclusion of replacement assets from “expansion” and the annual caps on improvements under section 14, the law must decide whether major refurbishment qualifies, on what conditions, and how the 200% interacts with the section 14 deduction.

3. What is “qualifying capital expenditure”? Is it confined to depreciable assets, or does it extend to land development, lease premiums, pre-operational costs, financing costs and intangibles? Will buildings on leasehold land continue to qualify?

4. How is the $ 3 million measured? For an expansion, is the test the expansion alone or the company’s total investment? Which exchange rate and which date apply when spending is in rupees over three to five years?

5. When does the clock start? Must the investment commence after the amending law is enacted, and how do the three- and five-year windows align with the existing implementation period?

6. Where will the allowance sit, and will the losses survive? Section 9(2) permits no concession except as provided in the Act. If the allowance sits outside the Second Schedule, the 10 year loss carry-forward may not apply and the six-year limit in section 19 could take over. As a 200% allowance will almost always create early losses, the carry forward loss provision is vital, and clarity is required whether it’s 6 years or more.

7. How does the election (option to choose) work? When should such election be made ? Should it be in writing and is it subject to approval ? Is it irrevocable, and how does it apply to BOI enterprises part-way through a Second Schedule project?

8. What happens on sale or failure? A specific recapture rule is needed if the allowance covers expenditure that is not a depreciable asset, together with a clear clawback where the threshold or sector conditions are not met.

These questions are not exhaustive, but answering them would give investors the clarity and certainty the incentive needs.

From Budget proposal to law

The policy logic holds: an allowance tied to capital actually spent is a better tool than a profit-based holiday, and it sits more comfortably with today’s global tax standards. But Sri Lanka has introduced, expired, extended and re-tiered its enhanced capital allowances repeatedly in recent years. Investors committing $ 3 million or more over a three- to five-year horizon need certainty more than generosity.

Past experience gives reason for caution. Sri Lanka has seen gaps open between what the policy maker intended, the language the legal draftsman chose and the way the tax administrator later interpreted it. Those gaps have caused real turmoil for taxpayers who committed capital in good faith, trusting that genuine investment would receive the promised incentive, only to find the benefit narrowed, delayed or disputed. An incentive that ends in litigation is no incentive at all; it erodes the very confidence it was meant to build. The policy maker must therefore ensure that the intent behind this proposal is carried into the law in clear and unambiguous terms.

The Tax Expenditure Statement 2025/2026, published by the Ministry of Finance on 12 November 2026, recognises enhanced and accelerated capital allowances as a form of tax expenditure. Yet its inventory neither lists nor estimates the cost of the Second Schedule ECA, and the

$ 250,000 tier introduced in 2026 is not disclosed as a new tax expenditure. If every concession is to be judged on the benefits it generates, the starting point must be to measure what existing allowances cost and what they have delivered. The 200% option proposed in the Budget 2027 should be costed and reported from the outset, so that its value for money can be tested rather than assumed.

A 200% allowance is a strong signal to investors. Whether it becomes a strong incentive, and for whom, depends entirely on the drafting and its implementation.

(The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in her personal capacity)

(Reference has been made to the Inland Revenue Act No 24 of 2017 and related amendments and the Budget Speech 2027.)

title: Electricity tariffs in Sri Lanka: Are consumers paying fair price? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 23 November 2026 00:20
-     - 108

Electricity is no longer merely a household necessity. It is a fundamental requirement for economic development, industrial competitiveness and improved living standards. As the world increasingly moves towards electric transportation, cooking and other technologies, access to affordable electricity has become more important than ever.

Despite achieving almost universal electricity access, Sri Lanka has relatively low per-capita electricity consumption compared with several countries in the region. According to World Bank data for 2024, Sri Lanka’s annual electricity consumption was approximately 695 units per person, compared with 1,223 units in India, 3,080 units in Thailand and 5,418 units in Malaysia.

This raises an important question: Are Sri Lankans consuming less electricity because they do not need it, or because they cannot afford it?

Although income levels, industrial development and economic activities influence electricity consumption, affordability is undoubtedly an important consideration. For many Sri Lankan families, the monthly electricity bill can represent a substantial financial burden, limiting their ability to enjoy the benefits of modern electrical appliances and technologies.

Unfortunately, Sri Lanka’s complicated electricity tariff structure, with its multiple consumption blocks, steep increases in charges and cross-subsidies, can discourage electricity consumption rather than promote improved living standards.

Electricity should be treated as an essential driver of economic development, not as a luxury to be discouraged through excessive pricing.

Does the present tariff penalise consumers?

One of the main weaknesses of Sri Lanka’s domestic electricity tariff is its progressive block-rate structure, under which electricity becomes increasingly expensive as monthly consumption increases.

Consider the domestic tariff effective from 11 May, 2026. A household consuming 180 units during a standard 30-day billing period pays Rs. 6,420, including the fixed charge. However, consuming just one additional unit increases the bill to Rs. 8,450.

In other words, a single additional unit of electricity increases the monthly bill by Rs. 2,030.

This occurs because crossing the 180-unit threshold changes not only the rate for additional electricity but also the charges applicable to the first 180 units and the monthly fixed charge.

A household consuming 350 units pays Rs. 25,350, equivalent to an average of Rs. 72.43 per unit. This is approximately twice the recent estimated national average cost of supplying electricity, which has varied around Rs. 30-37 per unit.

Although the national average cost does not necessarily represent the precise cost of supplying each consumer, such substantial differences raise legitimate questions about whether the existing tariff structure fairly reflects supply costs.


A large family, a household caring for elderly people or one with greater electricity requirements may easily fall into a higher consumption category without necessarily having a higher income.

Meanwhile, a wealthy household equipped with rooftop solar may purchase relatively little electricity from the grid and consequently qualify for a lower tariff category. Similarly, a luxury holiday bungalow occupied for only a few days each month may benefit from a low-consumption tariff despite the owner’s financial capacity.

These examples demonstrate that electricity consumption is not a reliable measure of household income.

Furthermore, high electricity charges can discourage families from using appliances that improve comfort, health and living standards. They may also discourage the transition from fossil-fuel-based cooking and transportation towards electricity.

Sri Lanka should encourage efficient and productive electricity consumption as part of national development rather than penalise consumers merely for using more electricity.

Cross-subsidies: Are we helping the right consumers?

Cross-subsidisation is another important concern. Under this arrangement, certain consumer categories pay higher tariffs to help compensate for lower tariffs charged to others.

Although the intention is often to protect low-income households or support important industries, the benefits are not necessarily received by those who genuinely need financial assistance.

The scale of this issue is significant. In June 2022, the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) reported that approximately 3.14 million domestic consumers, representing around 50% of domestic electricity connections at that time, consumed fewer than 60 units per month.

While many of these consumers genuinely required assistance, low electricity consumption alone could not establish their financial circumstances. The present distribution of consumers should be reassessed using updated data.

When tariffs are set below the actual cost of supplying a consumer category, the resulting revenue shortfall must ultimately be recovered through higher charges on other consumers, Government funding or losses incurred by the electricity utilities.

Such arrangements can place an unfair burden on consumers who pay substantially more than the cost attributable to their electricity supply.

The fundamental problem is the assumption that low electricity consumption necessarily indicates poverty, while high consumption indicates wealth.

Social welfare and industrial development are legitimate national objectives. However, financing these objectives should primarily be the responsibility of the Government rather than an obligation imposed indirectly on other electricity consumers.

Singapore provides a useful example. Eligible households receive Government-funded U-Save rebates credited directly to their utility accounts, based on defined eligibility criteria.

Sri Lanka could adopt a similar arrangement through the existing Aswesuma welfare framework, supported by appropriate verification of household income and circumstances. Eligible households could receive a Government-funded monthly electricity allowance, either through direct payments or credits to their electricity bills.


Likewise, if certain industries deserve assistance because of their contribution to employment, exports or national development, such support should be provided through transparent and targeted Government incentives rather than hidden cross-subsidies.

Sri Lanka already provides Government funding within its tariff arrangements. For example, the May 2026 tariff determination recognised a Government subsidy of Rs. 15 billion to protect selected consumer categories from tariff increases. However, eligibility was based principally on tariff categories and consumption thresholds rather than individual financial circumstances.

The objective should therefore be to replace broad, consumption-based subsidies progressively with better-targeted Government assistance, ensuring that those who genuinely need support receive it without unnecessarily burdening other consumers or the utilities.

Replace complicated block tariffs with simple, cost-reflective pricing

Sri Lanka should progressively replace its complicated consumption-block structure with a simpler tariff based on the efficient cost of supplying electricity.

Under an average-cost-based approach, consumers could pay a transparent energy charge reflecting the cost of electricity supply, together with a reasonable fixed or capacity charge to recover the cost of maintaining the network and providing a reliable connection.

Tariffs should primarily reflect factors that genuinely influence supply costs, including voltage level, contracted capacity, network requirements and time of consumption.

For example, supplying electricity to an industrial consumer at 11 kV or 33 kV involves different distribution costs from supplying a household at 230 V. Similarly, maintaining a high-capacity connection imposes infrastructure costs even when relatively little electricity is consumed.

These differences should be reflected transparently in electricity tariffs rather than through excessive reliance on the purpose of consumption or arbitrary consumption thresholds.

Malaysia provides a useful regional example through its revised tariff structure, which places greater emphasis on supply voltage and identifiable cost components.

A simplified tariff would allow consumers to understand what they are paying for while enabling utilities to recover the reasonable cost of the services they provide.

However, the transition should be gradual, with appropriate protection for vulnerable consumers and measures to avoid sudden increases in electricity bills.

Why should consumers pay for forecasting errors?

Another important concern is the heavy dependence on forecast revenue requirements when determining electricity tariffs.

Electricity generation costs are highly sensitive to rainfall, reservoir storage, hydropower availability, fuel prices, exchange rates, electricity demand and generating-plant availability.

These factors can change considerably within a short period, making accurate forecasting difficult.

An examination of recent PUCSL tariff determinations indicates that the average allowable cost of supplying electricity to consumers was approximately Rs. 32.63 per unit in 2024 and Rs. 29.55 per unit in 2025, while estimates for the middle of 2026 were higher, at around Rs. 37 per unit. These are overall supply-cost estimates or regulatory benchmarks, including generation, transmission, distribution and other approved costs, rather than generation costs alone.

Importantly, these figures demonstrate how electricity supply costs can vary considerably between periods.

Regulatory records also show significant differences between forecast and actual expenditure. For example, actual generation-energy expenditure during the first quarter of 2025 was approximately Rs. 9 billion below the amount initially forecast by PUCSL.

These variations highlight the importance of giving greater weight to verified actual expenditure rather than relying predominantly on uncertain future projections.

A more transparent approach would be to use verified actual costs from the preceding comparable period as the principal reference, supplemented by seasonal comparisons and clearly justified adjustments for expected changes.

The regulator should publish quarterly statements showing actual generation costs, purchased-power expenses, transmission and distribution costs, electricity sales and revenue, together with explanations of differences between earlier forecasts and actual expenditure.

Malaysia’s Automatic Fuel Adjustment mechanism offers a useful example. It allows monthly adjustments to reflect variations in fuel-related generation costs, resulting in additional charges or rebates depending on prevailing conditions.

Sri Lanka could adopt a similar transparent adjustment mechanism while maintaining appropriate financial safeguards for the utilities.

Forecasting cannot be eliminated entirely, particularly in a power system heavily influenced by hydropower and fuel-price variations. However, forecasting differences should be openly reconciled, and consumers should receive the benefits when actual costs are lower.

Importantly, inefficient operations, unnecessary expenditure and avoidable losses should not automatically be passed on to consumers merely because utilities have incurred those costs.

Tariff determination should be based on efficiently incurred and justifiable expenditure, supported by independent regulatory scrutiny.

Encourage rooftop solar without undermining utility financial sustainability

Rooftop solar has become an important national energy resource, attracting private investment, reducing dependence on conventional generation and contributing to energy security.

However, its continued development should not compromise the financial sustainability of electricity utilities, which must maintain the electricity network and ensure reliable supply even when solar generation is unavailable.


Countries such as Malaysia, Australia and the United Kingdom allow consumers to use their own solar electricity and export surplus generation to the grid. Consumers receive payments or credits for exported electricity while continuing to contribute towards the cost of maintaining the electricity network.

California has introduced a system under which export payments reflect the value of electricity to the power system, encouraging battery storage and electricity supply during higher-value periods.

Sri Lanka should adopt a similarly balanced approach rather than restricting new rooftop solar consumers exclusively to the Net Plus arrangement.

Consumers should have the option to use their own generation, store surplus energy in batteries and export excess electricity at a reasonable price reflecting the value of that electricity to the power system.

At the same time, a fair connection or capacity charge could ensure that solar consumers contribute towards maintaining the grid without transferring an unreasonable financial burden to other consumers.

As smart-metering infrastructure improves, higher payments could be offered for electricity exported during peak-demand periods, encouraging battery investment and reducing dependence on expensive conventional generation.

Such arrangements must also respect technical limitations, including voltage control, network capacity and grid stability.

The guiding principle should be simple: Consumers should pay fairly for using the electricity network, while utilities should pay fairly for the electricity consumers supply.

This would encourage rooftop solar investment while protecting both electricity utilities and non-solar consumers.

Introduce dynamic electricity pricing progressively

The cost of supplying electricity varies considerably throughout the day. During periods of abundant solar generation and relatively low demand, electricity can be less expensive, whereas during the evening peak, more costly thermal generation may be required.

Electricity tariffs should recognise these differences and encourage consumers to shift flexible electricity consumption towards lower-cost periods.

Malaysia has improved its Time-of-Use (TOU) tariff arrangements by offering lower rates during off-peak periods, while India has introduced Time-of-Day pricing provisions to encourage electricity consumption during solar-generation hours.

More advanced arrangements are available in Singapore and the United Kingdom, where participating consumers can choose electricity pricing that varies every half-hour.

Sri Lanka already offers optional TOU tariffs for domestic, commercial and industrial consumers. Therefore, the immediate priority should be to improve these existing arrangements rather than to introduce sophisticated real-time pricing prematurely.

Current TOU periods should be reviewed against actual generation costs, particularly to recognise the benefits of abundant daytime solar electricity.

Attractive tariffs during lower-cost periods could encourage electric-vehicle charging, water pumping, battery storage and other flexible electricity uses, helping to reduce evening peak demand.

As smart-metering infrastructure expands, more advanced dynamic tariffs could be introduced voluntarily, initially for high-consumption households, commercial establishments and consumers equipped with solar and battery systems.

However, reliable metering, transparent pricing, advance information and protection against excessive price volatility would be essential. Consumers who prefer predictable electricity bills should retain the option of conventional tariffs.

This gradual approach would improve the utilisation of existing generating capacity, accommodate greater renewable energy penetration and potentially postpone unnecessary investment in additional generation and network infrastructure.

A practical way forward for Sri Lanka

International experience demonstrates that electricity tariffs can be modernised without compromising consumer protection or the financial sustainability of utilities.

However, Sri Lanka cannot simply replicate systems adopted by countries with more advanced electricity markets. Reforms must reflect the country’s economic circumstances, institutional arrangements and existing infrastructure.

The immediate priority should be an independently reviewed cost-of-service study to determine the efficient cost of supplying electricity at different voltage levels and to different consumer categories.

This should be accompanied by regular publication of actual electricity supply costs, transparent tariff calculations and clear reconciliation of forecasting differences.

The complicated consumption-block structure and hidden cross-subsidies should then be progressively removed, while direct Government-funded assistance is established for eligible low-income households and strategically important industries.

Simpler tariffs based on supply voltage, capacity and electricity consumption should be introduced gradually, with appropriate safeguards against sudden increases in household bills.

In parallel, rooftop solar consumers should receive fair choices for self-consumption, storage and export, while improved TOU tariffs should encourage electricity use during lower-cost periods.

More advanced dynamic pricing arrangements can follow as smart-metering and other supporting infrastructure become available.

Throughout this transition, independent regulation will remain essential to protect consumers, ensure reliable electricity supply and prevent inefficient or unjustified costs from being passed on to the public.

Conclusion: Electricity should be an engine of development, not a luxury

Sri Lanka needs an electricity tariff structure that is fair, transparent, affordable and supportive of national economic development.

The objective should not merely be to recover utility revenue, but to provide reliable electricity at reasonable prices while ensuring the long-term financial sustainability of the power sector.

Electricity consumption should not be discouraged through punitive block tariffs, nor should consumers be expected to finance social welfare and industrial policies through hidden cross-subsidies.

Low-income households and deserving industries should receive transparent, Government-funded assistance. Tariff calculations should give greater importance to verified actual costs, with justified adjustments and proper reconciliation. Rooftop solar investment and flexible electricity consumption should be encouraged through fair and practical arrangements.

These reforms should be introduced progressively, protecting vulnerable consumers and avoiding sudden financial difficulties for electricity utilities.

The guiding principle should be straightforward: Electricity utilities should recover the efficient cost of the services they provide; the Government should finance the subsidies it wishes to grant; and consumers should be free to use electricity productively without being unfairly penalised.

A fair electricity tariff is not necessarily the cheapest. It is one that consumers can understand, utilities can sustain and the country can rely upon to improve living standards and accelerate economic development.

(The author is a former Chief Operating Officer of Electricity Distribution Lanka Ltd.)

The new arrangement provides the Lankan youngsters with two competitive fixtures, allowing them to build momentum and improve their chances of advancing.

The revised schedule comes at a particularly important time for the Sri Lankan camp, which experienced a delay of nearly two weeks in finalising the national squad following the NEXT XV Schools Franchise Rugby Tournament. The delay in the selection process had affected the preparation timeline, leaving the coaching staff with limited time to settle combinations and build a cohesive outfit ahead of the Asian championship. The change in format, however, has provided some relief, giving Sri Lanka an additional opportunity to compete and make their mark on the international stage.

Sri Lanka will open their campaign against Taipei on 11 December at the CR and FC ground in Longden Place. The opening fixture will be a must-win encounter for the hosts, who will be expected to make maximum use of home advantage and secure a positive result before facing the more formidable Hong Kong China outfit. The revised format makes the opening game even more important, as a strong performance could put Sri Lanka in a favourable position heading into the decisive final encounter.

Hong Kong China will take on Taipei on 15 December at the same venue, before Sri Lanka meet Hong Kong China on 19 December in what is expected to be the tournament’s defining fixture.
